cit.q: seeing that the post has been ruined in the noisy shed [for elephant bulls]...
entiram cilaikkum tuñcāk kampalai / vicayam aṭūum pukai cūḻ ālaitoṟum / karumpiṉ tīm cāṟu virumpiṉir micaimiṉ

You, who desired [it], enjoy the sweet juice of the sugarcane of all the halls surrounded by smoke, where the jaggery is being boiled, where the clamour does not cease, and where the machines resound!
the fire at the sheds fragrant from dark sugarcanes
aṟai uṟṟ' / ālaikk' alamarum tīm kaḻaik karumpē
the sugarcane with sweet stalks, which whirl in the sheds [for pressing] after being cut/being beaten (aṟai uṟṟu)
the sounds of sugarcane that is rapidly crushed at [its] stalks in all the sheds that looked like rain clouds
cit.note: The shed is possibly compared to a rain cloud because it is dark (with smoke from the boiling), it roars (with the noise of crushing), and it is full of liquid (the sweet juice, like rain).

note.p: A borrowing from Sanskrit śālā 'hall, house, shed' (NWS), denoting a shed or hall attached to a household. Its specific function is not lexically fixed but determined by context. In Classical Tamil texts it most commonly refers to a sugarcane mill, i.e. the shed in which cane was crushed and its juice boiled down into sugar, the press itself being called entiram (from Skt. yantra). Elsewhere it denotes a stable.

The sugarcane context is well attested, cf. Perumpāṇāṟṟuppaṭai 260–262: entiram cilaikkum tuñcāk kampalai vicayam aṭūum pukai cūḻ ālaitoṟum karumpiṉ tīm cāṟu; Paṭṭiṉappālai 9–10: kārk karumpiṉ kamaḻ ālait tī 'the fire at the sheds fragrant from dark sugarcanes'; Cilappatikāram line 151: poṅk' aḻi ālaip pukaiyoṭum 'together with the smoke from the sheds of boiling and crushing'. This usage closely parallels Sanskrit and Pali terms for sugarcane-processing sheds, such as īkṣuśālā and yantraśālā in the Avadānaśataka (tale 41) and ucchusālā in Buddhaghosa's Atthasālinī.
The mediaeval commentaries on 19: 23, 260–262 and Maturaikkāñci 258 gloss ālai as 'press'. This probably reflects a later shift from the building to the device it housed.

The word is also attested in an eleventh-century inscription on the walls of the Vīrattāṉēśvara shrine at Kīḻūr, near Tirukkōyilūr (South Indian Inscriptions, vol. 7, no. 863; p. 434 = A.R. No. 236 of 1902; digital edition: DHARMA, SII 7.863). Describing the surroundings, the text reads: veḷ pūm karump' iṭai tuṇittaratt' āṭṭ' oli ālai ayalatu 'in the vicinity of the shed [with] the grinding noise (āṭṭ' oli) [caused] by those who cut the white-flowered sugarcane in the middle' (transl. Ferenczi). Here, too, ālai denotes the building in which sugarcane was crushed, and the verb āṭṭu- 'to grind, crush' describes the process.
